claims.text: The Cr-free Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the Cr-free alloy are caused by dendritic versus interdendritic micro-segregation.
The Cr-free alloy has significantly lower room-temperature fracture strain than theoretically expected or reported for similar alloys.
The proposed intervention adds approximately 4 at.% Cr.
A sub-solvus annealing or aging treatment allows BCC decomposition and promotes secondary-phase formation in interdendritic regions.
Adding Cr induces a complex multicomponent Laves phase in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The Cr-induced Laves phase has a volume fraction of approximately 4%.
The Laves phase is primarily interdendritic and has a reticulated, interconnected morphology.
The Laves phase has a C14 or C15 crystal structure.
The reticulated Laves phase acts as a crack-deflection barrier that impedes crack extension.
Cr addition lowers the local mixing entropy in interdendritic regions.
Cr alters the local valence electron concentration, thereby helping drive TCP Laves-phase formation.
Lattice distortion from Cr dissolved in the BCC matrix produces solid-solution hardening.
The interconnected Laves-phase network provides a continuous brittle path that facilitates crack propagation.
Cr addition produces a net reduction in room-temperature fracture strain relative to the Cr-free baseline.
Cr solid-solution hardening and Laves-phase precipitation increase yield strength and hardness.
The Laves phase will cause detectable broadening or splitting of XRD peaks.
Cr substitution contracts the BCC lattice because Cr has a smaller atomic radius than Hf and Zr.
Approximately 4 vol% Laves phase is below the threshold for catastrophic percolation but above the threshold for effective crack deflection.

Comparing identically processed Cr-free and 4 at.% Cr alloys while measuring phase identity, morphology, lattice parameter, crack path, strength, and fracture strain can discriminate Cr-specific phase formation from pre-existing micro-segregation.

contradictions.description: The reticulated Laves phase is described both as a crack-deflection barrier that impedes extension and as a continuous brittle path that facilitates crack propagation; the conditions under which behavior switches between these roles are not operationally defined.

The hypothesis says the interconnected Laves network creates a percolation path that dominates fracture, whereas the boundary says approximately 4 vol% remains below the percolation threshold for catastrophic failure.

The boundary assigns approximately 4 vol% to a specific window between crack-deflection and catastrophic-percolation thresholds, while the uncertainty field states that the critical volume fraction is not established.
